newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Zaire troops go on looting spree in eastern town.
newsitem.headline: Zaire troops go on looting spree in eastern town.

text.p: Zairean soldiers went on a looting rampage in the eastern border town of Uvira on Tuesday, robbing foreign aid workers at gunpoint, residents said.
"There was a lot of shooting in the air, looting and general chaos," Chris Anderson of Care International told Reuters in Bujumbura, Burundi's capital just across the border from Uvira.
Aid agencies in radio contact with their staff in Uvira said troops took to the streets at about 7.30 a.m. (0530 gmt) and the looting and robbing spree lasted four hours.

Uvira was quiet by mid-afternoon and no casualties were reported among foreign aid workers. But Anderson said the soldiers stole two Care vehicles and other equipment and robbed staff of all their money.
Anderson and other Burundi-based aid officials said there were no immediate plans to evacuate staff.
"We have not reached that point yet," one said.
Zaire's ragged army is notoriously indisciplined. Soldiers say their irregular pay is a pittance and they have no choice but to turn to crime to survive.
But their chief, President Mobutu Sese Seko, is not in the country to impose his limited authority. Mobutu is still in Switzerland after surgery with no firm date for his return.
Unconfirmed reports said the looting was by men flown to eastern Zaire last month from the capital Kinshasa as reinforcements.
The region is tense because of a growing conflict between the army and the Banyamulenge people, ethnic Tutsis who arrived about 200 years ago from what are today Rwanda and Burundi.

Local Zairean authorities have whipped up public opinion against the Banyamulenge and diplomats fear the conflict could spread because the mainly Tutsi armies in Rwanda and Burundi may decide to support their kinfolk.

To add to the tension, more than one million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees live in camps in eastern Zaire and could potentially be sucked into the dispute with the ethnic Tutsis. About 210,000 of these refugees are in 11 camps in the Uvira region.
Foreign aid workers with U.N and private agencies gathered in the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) compound in Uvira during Tuesday's mayhem.
A special conty in and around the Hutu refugee camps, played a role in calming tempers and protecting aid workers, residents said.
As calm returned the aid staff left the UNHCR compound and spent the night in groups in their houses, aid officials said.
